summaries.gardner: Parker is a well-run, 100-plus-year-old industrial leader, not a Rule Breaker: its markets are mature, the brand is unknown to the public and it is not creating a new industry. It does show some Gardner traits, such as strong price momentum (+31% over the past year) and excellent management execution, but its growth of 4%-8% a year is far from the top-dog-in-an-emerging-industry profile.
summaries.buffett: Parker fits several Buffett tenets: an understandable business, 70 straight years of dividend increases, ROE of about 25%, free cash flow above net income ($3.9B vs $3.6B in FY2026) and diluted EPS up almost five-fold over ten years. Its moat rests on design-in switching costs and distribution rather than an unbeatable brand, and at about 34 times trailing earnings with debt rising after the $9.25B Filtration Group deal, the price leaves no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the quality of the operating system (the Win Strategy), the long record and the replacement-parts economics, and see few ways it could fail outright given its spread across about 1,000 markets. But it is a cyclical industrial with heavy acquisition goodwill ($11.1B) and a full price, so it is a good business at a fair-to-rich price rather than a wonderful business at a fair one.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms Parker is a stalwart with a simple story: sell more high-margin aerospace and replacement parts and keep lifting margins. The P/E of about 34 trailing (about 28 on FY2027 guidance) is well above its likely 8%-12% earnings growth, it is heavily covered by Wall Street, and insiders own little, so it fails his value tests even though the company is shrinking its share count.
summaries.fisher: Parker meets several of Fisher's points: a strong sales organization with about 18,300 distribution outlets, a management team that keeps lifting margins (adjusted segment margin 27.3% in FY2026) and long-lasting customer relationships. Its growth comes more from acquisitions and pricing than from breakthrough R&D, so it scores lower on Fisher's emphasis on new products driving many years of above-average growth.
summaries.graham: Parker passes Graham's size, earnings-stability and dividend tests: it is a large company, profitable every year for the past decade, with 70 consecutive years of dividend increases and EPS up from $5.89 to $28.48 in ten years. It fails clearly on price, at about 37 times average three-year earnings and a P/E times P/B of roughly 267 versus Graham's limit of 22.5.
summaries.thiel: Parker does not fit Zero to One: it has no technology ten times better than rivals, did not start by monopolizing a small niche and competes with large, capable firms such as Bosch Rexroth, Danfoss and SMC. Its strengths are distribution, durability and execution, which Thiel values less than proprietary breakthroughs and secret insights.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders with improving fundamentals at sensible valuations; Parker has rising margins, record backlog ($12.8B) and consistent earnings beats. Its revenue growth is modest and its valuation (about 27 times forward earnings, 3.2% free-cash-flow yield) already reflects much of that quality, and it is not a leading beneficiary of AI or another major platform shift.
summaries.druckenmiller: Parker has the earnings momentum Druckenmiller likes, with adjusted EPS up 18% in FY2026, six straight quarterly beats and orders rising 12% in Q4, plus clear catalysts such as Filtration Group synergies. Its cyclical, rate-sensitive and now more leveraged balance sheet makes it a macro-dependent industrial rather than a high-conviction, concentrated bet on a big secular change.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would like Parker's resilience, long record and strong cash conversion, but its returns (ROIC of about 16%, gross margin 37.7%) are below the 20%-plus returns and high gross margins of his typical holdings, and its growth depends heavily on acquisitions and the industrial cycle. At about 31 times free cash flow it is not cheap, so it is a good company that only partly fits his 'buy good companies, don't overpay' rule.
summaries.greenblatt: Parker earns a good return on capital (about 16% ROIC), but its earnings yield is low: operating profit of about $5.1B is only about 3.9% of its roughly $130B enterprise value. It would not rank near the top of Greenblatt's Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: On Akre's three-legged stool, Parker has a quality business with decent returns and a capable, shareholder-minded management team. The weaker leg is reinvestment: capex is only about 2% of sales, so it compounds mainly by buying companies, such as Filtration Group at 19.6 times EBITDA, which earn lower initial returns.
summaries.pabrai: Parker is a simple, established business with low risk of permanent loss, but it is not a Dhandho bet: there is no temporary, fixable setback and the stock trades near record highs at about 34 times trailing earnings. The 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' asymmetry Pabrai seeks is missing at this price.
summaries.wood: Parker is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing, and its costs are not falling rapidly with volume. Its electrification work (such as Curtis Instruments) is a small part of a mature industrial business, so it fits Wood's approach poorly.
summaries.ackman: Parker matches many of Ackman's criteria: a simple, predictable, cash-generative business with high barriers to entry through design-in and distribution, solid management and a record of margin gains. It is more cyclical and exposed to industrial demand and tariffs than his favorite royalty-like businesses, and the current price leaves less room for upside than he usually requires.
summaries.sleep: Parker uses its scale mostly to raise margins rather than share the savings with customers, so it lacks Sleep's 'scale economies shared' flywheel. Its position in 10 to 20 years should be durable but not clearly far stronger than today, so it is a solid compounder rather than a Nomad-style holding.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets and products solving painful problems; Parker solves real engineering problems for machine and aircraft makers, but in mature markets growing at mid-single digits. It is a long-established industrial, not the kind of young company riding a big new technology wave that Sequoia targets.
summaries.nash: Parker is a high-quality, large industrial outside Nash's zones to avoid, with strong profitability (about 24% operating margin), low short interest and consistent beats, but it fails several of his hard tests. Revenue growth of 8.3% is below 10%, debt far exceeds cash, growth plus free-cash-flow margin is only about 26, and his DCF shows a value well below today's price, so it scores about 70 of 130 and is not a buy under his method.
